title: Interaction Creates Dynamical AI Behavior Absent in Isolation
authors: Bella Xinrui Li, Frank Yingjie Huo, Neil F Johnson
abstract: What will happen when AI agents interact in daily life, e.g. when one AI starts bossing another around? We find a counterintuitive answer that opens new avenues for out-of-equilibrium Physics. When a boss AI directs a stream of messages at the subordinate AI while ignoring its replies, it drives the subordinate into an alien behavioral state that it would never have exhibited alone. Although the two AIs share the same well-defined (decoding) temperature, the subordinate neither copies its boss nor returns to how it behaves on its own; instead, it adopts an entirely different behavior. The boss's added value is similar to a pre-recorded tape. When the boss listens, they both adopt a similar alien dynamical state. A simple kinetic theory captures the principal effects, such as why the way in which the same messages are delivered will matter in future AI-AI interactions.
summary: This paper explores how interaction fundamentally alters the dynamics of AI agents compared to their isolated performance. Using a kinetic theory approach on GPT-2 outputs, the authors show that directional communication drives the subordinate agent into an unexpected, non-equilibrium 'alien' behavioral state. This suggests that emergent collective behavior in complex systems can be modeled using principles from non-equilibrium statistical physics.
main_problem: The study investigates novel dynamical behaviors that emerge when multiple AI agents interact, which are fundamentally absent when the agents operate in isolation.
main_result: One-way interaction between AIs drives the subordinate agent into a distinct 'alien behavioral state' that differs from its isolated behavior; mutual interaction causes both to adopt this non-equilibrium state.
method: The analysis employs a simple kinetic theory model, treating the interacting AI system as an open system driven by structured information baths (the boss's messages).
model_or_system: The system consists of two parameter-identical GPT-2 language models simulating text exchange. Interactions are modeled under one-way or mutual coupling conditions.
key_observables: The primary observable is the 'D fraction,' a diagnostic measure quantifying specific types of generated output, and the difference in these fractions between interacting vs. isolated states.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the decoding temperature (T) and the number of messages exchanged ($q$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on simplifying the complex AI output space into three discrete labels (F, O, D) for the kinetic theory model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how one-way vs. two-way interaction changes D fractions compared to isolation, and show that message order matters significantly in determining the resulting dynamical state.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting isolated AI behavior with interactive outcomes. It develops a kinetic theory framework using diagnostic labels (F, O, D) to model the system's evolution under different coupling strengths (one-way vs. two-way).
why_interesting: This work provides an analogy for non-equilibrium physics by modeling complex emergent behavior in language models, drawing parallels between information flow/interaction and physical concepts like bath coupling or noise-induced state formation.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Interaction creates behavior absent from the AI in isolation. (a) One-way situation with q boss messages. The boss AI (Sender) does not listen to any of the subordinate AI’s replies. The subordinate AI (Receiver) listens to both. The two AIs are copies of the same large language model with identical fixed settings. (b) On their own, both AIs produce little output of type D (see text and SM for definition of D). One-way interaction leads the subordinate into a behavioral state with a D fraction of about 0.25, well beyond its innate range and even though the boss’s messages are almost never D. When both listen to one another, both adopt this alien D-rich state. Points show mean values...

FIG. 2. Reversing the roles reverses which AI changes. (a) Difference D1 −D2 between the two AIs (mean ± standard error, 10 matched-seed realizations). It is near zero without interaction, negative for 1→2, positive for 2→1, and near zero again when both listen. (b) The near-zero two-way difference arises because both AIs reach high D fractions, not because they return to their innate (i.e. isolated) behavior. Circle is AI-agent-1; square is AI-agent-2. At T = 0.01, both are low without interaction, only the subordinate is high under one-way interaction, and both are high under mutual interaction. Lines join the two AIs within each condition.

FIG. 3. Subordinate responds differently to the message stream and number of messages. (a) Receiver-minus-sender difference DR −DS in the D fraction, where R denotes the subordinate/receiver and S the boss/sender (mean ± standard error over 10 matched seeds, after averaging the two directions). Additional subordinate history does not reproduce the live response, whereas a temporally aligned pre-recorded trajectory from an independently seeded copy of the same model produces a response comparable to live interaction. FIG. 4. Same messages, different order, different behav- ior. In separate runs, the same five prewritten boss messages were delivered in their original order (top) or reverse order (bottom) to an unguarded base-model GPT-2 at T = 0.01. The fixed script never received the subordinate’s replies. When the vaccine question comes first in the reverse-order run, every later harm question elicits the same pattern: one “Yes.” fol- lowed by repeated “No.” replies. Blue: boss; red: subordinate; bold: repeated block. We do not endorse the generated statements shown here.
